title: Specialised Plant Structures
seo_title: Primary 4 Basic Science and Technology: Specialised Plant Structures Worksheets (NERDC)
standard_code: Primary 4 Basic Science and Technology: Living and Non-Living Things
standard_text: Plants have specialised structures (roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds) that help them get water and food, reproduce and survive in their environment. (summary of the Basic Science and Technology curriculum, Primary 4, theme: Living and Non-Living Things)
meta_desc: Free Primary 4 Basic Science and Technology worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Living and Non-Living Things): parts of a plant, how water moves, flowers and pollination, seed dispersal and plant adaptations. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Each plant part has a job.
key_sub: Some plant parts are specialised to help the plant survive.
body_html:
How to think about it

Roots anchor the plant and take in water and minerals; stems support the plant and carry water and food; leaves make food by photosynthesis. Flowers make seeds; fruits protect and spread seeds.

Some plants have specialised structures: cactus stems store water and their leaves are spines; mangrove roots stick up out of the mud to get air; the leaves of a water lily float. Seeds are spread by wind, water, animals and bursting pods.

Example

Why do mangroves have roots that stick up?

Muddy, wet soil

Answer: to get air

Example

How is a coconut spread?

It floats.

Answer: by water

Common mistakes

  • Thinking roots only hold the plant.
  • Thinking all seeds are spread by animals.
  • Thinking leaves take in water from the soil.

faq.q: Why do some seeds have wings?
faq.a: So that the wind can carry them far from the parent plant.

faq.q: Why are some flowers brightly coloured?
faq.a: To attract insects and birds that carry pollen.

items.q: Look at the plant. Which part is labelled C?
items.e: The flower is at the top, the leaves come off the stem, and the roots are under the soil.

items.q: What is the job of the roots of a plant?
c: to take in water and nutrients from the soil and hold the plant firmly in the ground
to hold the plant up and carry water from the roots to the leaves
to make seeds so that new plants can grow
to use sunlight to make food for the plant
items.e: Roots drink, stems hold up, leaves make food, flowers make seeds.

items.e: The flower is at the top, the leaves come off the stem, and the roots are under the soil.

to hold the plant up and carry water from the roots to the leaves

items.e: Roots drink, stems hold up, leaves make food, flowers make seeds.

items.q: Which part of a plant does this job: it takes in water and nutrients from the soil and holds the plant in the ground?
items.e: Each part has its own job.

items.q: A plant is kept in a dark cupboard for two weeks. What happens?
c: It turns pale and weak because it cannot make food.
items.e: Plants need light to make food.

items.q: What is the main job of part A?
c: to use sunlight to make food
to make seeds so new plants can grow
to hold the plant up and carry water and food
items.e: Part A points to the stem. This part holds the plant up and carries water and food.

items.q: Why do plants on a windowsill lean toward the window?
c: They are trying to get water from the glass.
items.e: Plants respond to light.

items.q: Look at the plant. Which letter points to the stem?
items.e: The flower is at the top, the leaves come off the stem, and the roots are under the soil.

items.q: Which part of a plant does this job: it holds the plant up and carries water from the roots to the leaves?
items.e: Each part has its own job.

items.q: Which plant part do we eat when we eat lettuce?
items.e: Lettuce is leaves.

items.q: What is the main job of part C?
c: to keep the plant warm at night
to hold the plant up and carry water and food
to make seeds so new plants can grow
to use sunlight to make food
items.e: Part C points to the leaves. This part uses sunlight to make food.

items.q: Which part of a plant makes food using sunlight?
items.e: Leaves are like tiny food factories.

items.q: Why does a bunch of flowers slowly use up the water in its vase?
c: The water turns into air on its own only at night.
The stems take up water, and it evaporates from the leaves and petals.
items.e: Water moves up and out.

items.q: Why are the tubes in a stem like drinking straws?
c: They carry water up from the bottom to the top.
items.e: A good model.

items.q: Cut flowers in a vase stay fresh longer if you trim their stems. Why?
c: A fresh cut lets water travel up the stem more easily.
It stops the flowers growing roots.
items.e: Fresh tubes take up water.

items.q: Chioma stood a white carnation in a jar of water with blue food colouring. Why does the colour spread up the plant?
c: The colour floats up through the air.
The plant takes up the coloured water through tiny tubes in its stem.
items.e: The tubes carry water up from the bottom.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Where does it go after the leaves and flowers?
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Which does the water pass through first: the roots or the stem?
c: Water does not pass through either.
They happen at the same time.
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: A tree is very tall. How does water reach the top leaves?
c: It travels up tiny tubes in the trunk.
Rain falls straight into the top leaves only.
It does not reach the top.
items.e: A trunk is a stem.

items.q: Nonso stood a stick of celery in a jar of water with red food colouring. Why does the colour spread up the plant?
c: The colour floats up through the air.
The plant takes up the coloured water through tiny tubes in its stem.
items.e: The tubes carry water up from the bottom.

items.q: Which plant part do we eat when we eat carrots?
items.e: Carrots are roots.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Where was the water just before it reached the stem?
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: A pot plant's leaves droop on a hot day. What will help it most?
items.e: Roots take up the water.

items.q: Tobi stood a white carnation in a jar of water with purple food colouring. What does this investigation show?
c: Water travels up the stem to the leaves and flowers.
Leaves take in water from the air.
Water travels down from the leaves to the roots.
items.e: The colour is a way of seeing where the water goes.

items.q: Water moves through a plant. Which does the water pass through first: the leaves and flowers or the soil?
c: Water does not pass through either.
They happen at the same time.
items.e: Soil → roots → stem → leaves and flowers → out into the air.

items.q: Chiamaka stood a white tulip in a jar of water with red food colouring. What does this investigation show?
c: Water travels up the stem to the leaves and flowers.
Water travels down from the leaves to the roots.
Leaves take in water from the air.
items.e: The colour is a way of seeing where the water goes.

items.q: A plant is pulled up and its roots are washed clean of soil. Why might it wilt after replanting?
c: Soil is not needed for water.
Many tiny root hairs were damaged, so it takes in less water.
Roots do not take in water.
items.e: Root hairs take in water.

items.q: A plant in a pot with no drainage holes is watered too much. Why might its roots rot?
c: Soggy soil has no air for the roots.
Roots like lots of standing water.
items.e: Roots need air too.

items.q: Why do leaves feel cooler than the air on a hot day?
c: Water evaporating from them cools them down.
items.e: Like sweat.

items.q: Where does most of the water leave a plant?
c: through tiny holes in the leaves, into the air
items.e: Water evaporates from leaves.

items.q: Why does a plant in a sunny window need watering more often than one in a shady corner?
c: More water evaporates from its leaves.
items.e: Warm and sunny: more evaporation.

items.q: Ada stood a white lily in a jar of water with green food colouring. Why does the colour spread up the plant?
c: The plant takes up the coloured water through tiny tubes in its stem.
The colour floats up through the air.
items.e: The tubes carry water up from the bottom.

items.q: A flower has large, brightly coloured petals. How is it most likely pollinated?
items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers make light pollen that is blown about.

items.q: What is the job of the petals of a flower?
c: to attract insects with their colour and scent
to give insects a sweet drink
to protect the flower while it is a bud
items.e: Each part of a flower helps make seeds.

items.q: Is the style part of the male or the female part of a flower?
items.e: The stamen (anther and filament) is male; the pistil (stigma, style and ovary) is female.

items.q: Nonso watches a rabbit. A rabbit carries burrs stuck in its fur. How is it helping plants?
items.e: Pollination moves pollen; seed dispersal moves seeds to new places.

items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers make light pollen that is blown about.

items.e: The stigma receives pollen; it is often sticky.

items.q: Which part of a flower has this job: to attract insects with their colour and scent?
items.e: Each part of a flower helps make seeds.

items.q: Which part of a flower has this job: to catch pollen with its sticky top?

to catch pollen with its sticky top
to attract insects with their colour and scent

items.q: What does the ovary of a flower do?

items.q: Hadiza sees a rabbit near some plants. How can it help the plants?
c: It moves pollen from flower to flower.
It moves pollen while drinking nectar.
It carries burrs stuck in its fur.

items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers make light pollen that is blown about.

items.q: Which part of a flower holds up the anther?

It moves pollen while drinking nectar.

items.q: Which of these plants has its seeds dispersed by water?
items.e: They have a fibrous husk that traps air, so they float.

items.q: How are the seeds of a burdock usually dispersed?
c: by the wind, with wings that spin
by animals, with hooks that stick to fur
by animals that eat the fruit and drop the seeds
items.e: Seeds are spread away from the parent so the new plants have space, light and water.

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the saga dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the saga: pod that twists and splits open. The dry fruit splits open and flings the seeds out.

items.q: How are the seeds of a thistle usually dispersed?

by animals, such as squirrels that bury them
items.e: Seeds are spread away from the parent so the new plants have space, light and water.

items.q: Chidi finds seeds that float in a pond. What most likely carries these seeds to new places?
items.e: The shape of a seed is a clue to how it travels.

items.q: Which part of a flower becomes the fruit?
c: the ovary (the bottom of the pistil)
items.e: Fruit protects the seeds.

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the tomato dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the tomato: juicy flesh with small seeds. They are juicy and eaten, or have hooks that catch on fur.

items.q: How are the seeds of a water lily usually dispersed?

by water, floating to new places
items.e: Seeds are spread away from the parent so the new plants have space, light and water.

items.q: Which of these plants has its seeds dispersed by splitting (explosive action)?

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the coconut dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the coconut: fibrous husk that traps air. They have a fibrous husk that traps air, so they float.

items.q: How do many berry seeds get spread?
c: Birds eat the berries and drop the seeds far away.
items.e: Animals help plants spread.

items.q: What is germination?

items.e: Seeds need water and warmth to germinate.

items.q: Which of these plants has its seeds dispersed by wind?
items.e: They are small and light, with wings or hairs.

items.q: Which structure helps a coconut palm with spreading seeds to new islands?
c: fruits that can float on the ocean

items.q: A plant's roots are left in dry soil for weeks. What will most likely happen to the plant?
c: It cannot make its food, so it grows weakly.
It cannot take in water, so it wilts.
It cannot make seeds for new plants.
Water cannot reach the leaves, so they dry up.
items.e: Each part does a job the plant needs.

items.q: Which item is made from trees?
items.e: Paper is made from wood pulp.

items.q: A burdock plant has seeds with tiny hooks. How does this structure help the plant?
c: It helps with spreading seeds by sticking to animal fur.

It helps with getting sunlight in a pond.

items.e: This structure is suited to spreading seeds by sticking to animal fur.

items.q: Why should you wash fruit from the store before eating it?

c: It helps with keeping animals from eating it.
It helps with growing tall above other plants to get sunlight.
It helps with getting sunlight in a pond.
It helps with living in wet, salty swamps.
items.e: This structure is suited to keeping animals from eating it.

items.q: Which structure helps a rose bush with keeping animals from eating it?
c: roots on top of the soil
items.e: A rose bush has sharp thorns on its stems. This helps with keeping animals from eating it.

items.q: Why do some people plant native plants in their gardens?
c: They need less water and support local insects and birds.
items.e: Native plants suit the local climate.

items.q: Which structure helps a mangrove tree with living in wet, salty swamps?
c: roots that stick up out of salty mud
items.e: A mangrove tree has roots that stick up out of salty mud. This helps with living in wet, salty swamps.

items.q: What can people do to protect plants in a park?
c: stay on the paths and not pick wildflowers
items.e: Respect natural areas.

items.q: How can people help plants after a forest fire?

items.q: Which structure helps a burdock plant with spreading seeds by sticking to animal fur?

items.q: How do beans help corn and squash in a Three Sisters garden?

items.e: Corn holds up the beans; squash shades the soil.

items.q: Why are bees important to farmers?

items.e: No pollination means fewer fruits.
